- Girth ≥ 5 means no cycles of length 3 or 4
- A tree satisfies girth ≥ 5 trivially (no cycles)

I'll build a bipartite tree containing edges (0,1) and (0,8).

Partition: A = {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, B = {1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12}

Star from 0 to all of B, then add leaves from A side to nodes in B:
- (0,1), (0,8), (0,9), (0,10), (0,11), (0,12) — star
- (1,2), (1,3), (4,8), (5,8), (6,9), (7,9) — leaves

This gives 12 edges, is a tree (so girth = ∞ ≥ 5), and is bipartite.

Since bipartite graphs have no odd cycles, they automatically avoid odd-length cycles, so I just need to eliminate 4-cycles to achieve girth ≥ 5. A simple path structure like 0-1-2-3-...-12 would work as a starting point since paths have infinite girth, though I'll need to add edges carefully to reach the 8-edge minimum while maintaining the girth constraint.

When I try adding edge (0,8) to connect the endpoints, it creates a 9-cycle which is odd and breaks bipartiteness. The issue is that in a standard alternating coloring of the path, vertices 0 and 8 end up the same color. So I need to partition the vertices deliberately: placing 0 in one part (say A) and ensuring both 1 and 8 are in the other part (B). I'll set A = {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} and B = {1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12}, giving me 7 vertices on each side. Now I can add edges between A and B while avoiding 4-cycles—a star configuration from 0 to all of B gives me 6 edges, and I need to add a couple more edges between other vertices in A and B to reach 8 edges total without creating any 4-cycles.
